desc:
Given the integer positions nums on a number line, choose an integer x that minimizes

f(x) = |nums[0] - x|3 + |nums[1] - x|3 + ... + |nums[n-1] - x|3

and return it. If several integers give the same minimal value, return the smallest of them. The chosen point need not appear in nums.

Example: for [1, 2, 6] the answer is 3 (f(3) = 8 + 1 + 27 = 36, while f(2) = 1 + 0 + 64 = 65 and f(4) = 27 + 8 + 8 = 43).
hints: f is a sum of convex functions, so it is convex: it decreases, possibly stays flat for one step, then increases. Checking every x in the range works but is slow for wide ranges and large inputs.
For a convex function the differences f(x + 1) - f(x) are non-decreasing in x. The minimizer is where that difference first becomes non-negative.
Binary search the smallest integer x in [min(nums), max(nums)] with f(x + 1) - f(x) ≥ 0. Evaluating f costs O(n); sums reach about 3 * 1017, so use 64-bit integers.
editorial: Each term |a - x|3 is convex in x, and a sum of convex functions is convex, so the sequence of differences d(x) = f(x + 1) - f(x) is non-decreasing. A convex function is minimised exactly where d switches from negative to non-negative; the smallest x with d(x) ≥ 0 is therefore the smallest minimizer (if d(x) == 0, both x and x + 1 are optimal and we want the smaller one).

The optimum lies between the smallest and the largest input: outside that interval moving toward the data strictly decreases every term. At x = max(nums) the difference is positive (or all points are equal and it is positive as well), so the predicate is true at the right end of the search interval and the binary search is well defined. With about 15 iterations and an O(n) evaluation, the running time is O(n log R) where R is the width of the value range. Unlike the median (for absolute distance) or the mean (for squared distance), no closed form exists for cubes, which is why a monotone predicate is the tool.
